coverage: All four books and 48 local reading units in original-en and modern-en, including surviving footnotes. Named historical, philosophical, literary and religious references with scoped namesakes and identifiable implicit references. No invented personal identities for generic rulers, offices, assemblies or peoples; inherited truncated notes are documented for release review.

entities.name: Hugo Grotius
entities.body: The Dutch jurist whose arguments about sovereignty and slavery Rousseau challenges.

entities.name: Thomas Hobbes
entities.body: The English political philosopher discussed on authority and the relation of religion to government.

entities.name: Philo
entities.body: The Jewish philosopher from Alexandria cited as a source for Caligula’s reasoning.

entities.name: Caligula
entities.body: The Roman emperor used in examples about rulers’ claims to superiority.

entities.name: Aristotle
entities.body: The Greek philosopher cited on slavery, political authority and forms of government.

entities.name: The Marquis d’Argenson
entities.body: The French statesman whose political observations Rousseau quotes.

entities.name: François Rabelais
entities.body: The French satirist cited in the discussion of slavery.

entities.name: Cato the Elder
entities.body: The Roman statesman who writes about his son’s military oath.

entities.name: Cato’s son
entities.body: Marcus Porcius Cato Licinianus, the elder Cato’s son serving under Popilius.

entities.name: Cato the Younger
entities.body: The Roman republican statesman mentioned in the debate about Caesar’s speech.

entities.name: Popilius
entities.body: The Roman commander addressed by Cato about his son’s military service.

entities.name: Jean Bodin
entities.body: The French political thinker cited in the note on citizens and townsmen.

entities.name: Jean le Rond d’Alembert
entities.body: The French scholar cited on Geneva and on the discussion of public morals.

entities.name: Vasco Núñez de Balboa
entities.body: The Spanish explorer whose claim to territory illustrates the argument about possession.

entities.name: Jean Barbeyrac
entities.body: The jurist and translator of Grotius discussed in the note on sovereignty.

entities.name: Louis XIII
entities.body: The French king to whom Grotius dedicated his book.

entities.name: George I
entities.body: The British king to whom Barbeyrac dedicated his translation.

entities.name: James II
entities.body: The deposed British king mentioned in the argument about legitimate authority.

entities.name: William III
entities.body: The king whose succession is discussed alongside James II’s removal.

entities.name: Lycurgus
entities.body: The traditional Spartan lawgiver used as an example of founding institutions.

entities.name: Solon
entities.body: The Athenian lawgiver cited among founders of political institutions.

entities.name: Numa Pompilius
entities.body: The traditional second king of Rome, cited as a lawgiver.

entities.name: Servius Tullius
entities.body: The Roman king associated with the census and the organization of the voting assemblies.

entities.name: Montesquieu
entities.body: The French political philosopher cited on laws, government and climate.

entities.name: Plato
entities.body: The Greek philosopher whose political thought Rousseau discusses.

entities.name: John Calvin
entities.body: The religious reformer whose role in Geneva’s laws Rousseau praises.

entities.name: Niccolò Machiavelli
entities.body: The Florentine political writer whose advice to rulers Rousseau reads as instruction for the people.

entities.name: William Warburton
entities.body: The English bishop and writer cited on the relationship between politics and religion.

entities.name: Peter the Great
entities.body: The Russian tsar whose reforms Rousseau criticizes as premature imitation.

entities.name: René Descartes
entities.body: The French philosopher invoked in the discussion of political order.

entities.name: The Count Palatine
entities.body: The Polish nobleman quoted as preferring dangerous liberty to peaceful servitude.

entities.name: Archimedes
entities.body: The ancient mathematician used in a comparison about concentrated power.

entities.name: Dionysius the Younger
entities.body: The ruler of Syracuse who answers his father’s rebuke in the anecdote about royal upbringing.

entities.name: Dionysius the Elder
entities.body: The ruler of Syracuse who rebukes his son in the anecdote about kingship.

entities.name: Dionysius the Younger’s grandfather
entities.body: The non-royal grandfather invoked in the reply about inherited kingship.

entities.name: Cesare Borgia
entities.body: The Italian ruler whom Rousseau discusses as Machiavelli’s chosen example.

entities.name: Livy
entities.body: The Roman historian whose work appears in the title of Machiavelli’s Discourses.

entities.name: Jean Chardin
entities.body: The French traveler cited for observations on life in Persia.

entities.name: Cardinal de Retz
entities.body: The coadjutor of Paris mentioned in the account of political unrest in France.

entities.name: Tacitus
entities.body: The Roman historian quoted on government and political servility.

entities.name: Sulla
entities.body: The Roman general and dictator cited in the discussion of political decay.

entities.name: Julius Caesar
entities.body: The Roman general and statesman cited in the arguments about power and the republic.

entities.name: Augustus
entities.body: The first Roman emperor, cited in the account of the republic’s decline.

entities.name: Tiberius
entities.body: The Roman emperor who succeeded Augustus.

entities.name: Cornelius Nepos
entities.body: The Roman biographer cited on the meaning of tyranny.

entities.name: Miltiades
entities.body: The Athenian commander whose biography is cited in the note on tyranny.

entities.name: Xenophon
entities.body: The Greek writer whose Hiero is cited in discussing tyranny.

entities.name: Oliver Cromwell
entities.body: The English political and military leader used in examples about manipulation and power.

entities.name: The Duc de Beaufort
entities.body: The French nobleman invoked as a popular agitator in the comparison with Geneva.

entities.name: Otho
entities.body: The Roman emperor whose senators denounced his rival Vitellius.

entities.name: Vitellius
entities.body: Otho’s rival for the Roman imperial throne.

entities.name: The Abbé de Saint-Pierre
entities.body: The French political reformer whose proposal for royal councils Rousseau discusses.

entities.name: Varro
entities.body: The Roman writer cited on the rural foundations of the republic.

entities.name: Pliny the Elder
entities.body: The Roman writer cited on the standing of the rural voting tribes.

entities.name: Appius Claudius
entities.body: The Sabine migrant who became the ancestor of the Roman Claudian family.

entities.name: Romulus
entities.body: Rome’s legendary founder and first king.

entities.name: Gaius Marius
entities.body: The Roman general cited on army recruitment and civil conflict.

entities.name: Tarquin the Proud
entities.body: The last king of Rome, referred to as the later Tarquin.

entities.name: Cicero
entities.body: The Roman orator and consul discussed on voting, emergency powers and religion.

entities.name: Agis IV
entities.body: The Spartan king whose killing by the ephors is discussed.

entities.name: Cleomenes III
entities.body: The Spartan king mentioned in the account of the ephors and Sparta’s decline.

entities.name: Pompey
entities.body: The Roman general whose struggle with Caesar illustrates military power over civil authority.

entities.name: Catiline
entities.body: The Roman conspirator invoked in the discussions of dictatorship and civic loyalty.

entities.name: Pierre Bayle
entities.body: The French philosopher whose views on religion and society Rousseau examines.

entities.name: Henry IV
entities.body: The French king whose conversion to Catholicism is invoked in the argument about intolerance.

entities.name: Louis de Carrières
entities.body: The French biblical translator whose rendering of Jephthah’s words Rousseau questions.

entities.name: Adam
entities.body: The first man of the biblical creation story, invoked in the satirical discussion of inherited kingship.

entities.name: Noah
entities.body: The biblical patriarch used in the same argument about hereditary rule.

entities.name: Noah’s sons
entities.body: The three biblical sons of Noah, invoked as supposed founders of kingdoms.

entities.name: Saturn
entities.body: The Roman god invoked in comparing stories of divine and royal descent.

entities.name: Saturn’s children
entities.body: The divine children invoked in the comparison with Noah’s sons.

entities.name: Robinson Crusoe
entities.body: Defoe’s fictional island-dweller, used in an example of sovereignty without subjects.

entities.name: Ulysses
entities.body: Odysseus, the Homeric hero whose companions appear in the comparison about submission.

entities.name: Ulysses’s companions
entities.body: The men of the Homeric hero’s company used in Rousseau’s comparison.

entities.name: The Cyclops
entities.body: The man-eating giant from the Odyssey, invoked in the discussion of captivity.

entities.name: God
entities.body: The divine being invoked in the discussion of authority, obligation and civil religion.

entities.name: Ishmael
entities.body: The biblical son of Abraham invoked in the traditional ancestry of Muhammad.

entities.name: Muhammad
entities.body: The prophet of Islam whose combination of religious and political authority Rousseau discusses.

entities.name: Minos
entities.body: The legendary Cretan ruler associated with its laws.

entities.name: Hercules
entities.body: The classical hero used in a comparison about the demands of ruling.

entities.name: Samuel
entities.body: The biblical prophet who warns the Israelites about kingship.

entities.name: Moloch
entities.body: The deity named in Rousseau’s argument against conflating different peoples’ gods.

entities.name: Chronos
entities.body: The Greek divine figure named alongside Saturn in the argument against merging different gods.

entities.name: Baal
entities.body: The Phoenician deity distinguished from Greek Zeus and Roman Jupiter.

entities.name: Zeus
entities.body: The Greek chief god distinguished here from the gods of other peoples.

entities.name: Jupiter
entities.body: The Roman chief god, including the Jupiter worshipped on the Capitol.

entities.name: Moses
entities.body: The biblical lawgiver mentioned in discussing the God of Israel.

entities.name: Chamos
entities.body: Chemosh, the deity invoked in the quoted exchange with the Ammonites.

entities.name: Jephthah
entities.body: The biblical judge whose words about territorial rights Rousseau quotes.

entities.name: Jesus Christ
entities.body: The central figure of Christianity, discussed in relation to spiritual and political authority.

entities.name: Ali
entities.body: Muhammad’s cousin and son-in-law, the foundational figure invoked in discussing Shi‘a Islam.

entities.name: Homer
entities.body: The ancient Greek poet invoked through the depiction of gods taking sides in human wars.

entities.name: The Medici
entities.body: The Florentine ruling family whose court is mentioned in the discussion of Machiavelli.

entities.name: The Tarquins
entities.body: The Roman royal family whose expulsion is discussed.

entities.name: The Gracchi
entities.body: The Roman reforming brothers Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus, invoked in the discussion of popular representation.

entities.name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
entities.body: The author of The Social Contract, named in editorial notes on quotations.
